topic: Re-derive it. Don't take it on trust.

items.prompt: Why run a published study again instead of trusting it?

choices.text: Only running it again can say no

faster.note: The film says the opposite: trust is the fast option.

journal.note: No journal rule came into it. The point was what each option can show.

source.quote: Running it again is slow, and it is the only one of the two that can say no.

items.prompt: Of 97 positive psychology results run again in 2015, about how many came back significant?

most.note: This treats publication as a guarantee. The repeats came back far less often.

none.note: Some did come back, at about half their original size.

source.quote: Of those ninety-seven, thirty-five came back significant in the repeat.

items.prompt: Science required authors to share data and code on request. For what share of 204 papers did researchers get them?

choices.text: All of them, since it was required

all.note: A rule that relies on the author answering does not make every author answer.

ten.note: The share was much higher than that, and still under half.

source.quote: They got the materials for forty-four percent of the papers

items.prompt: What let researchers check 240 million web certificates without asking anyone?

choices.text: They checked a small sample and guessed

issuers.note: The point of this case is that no issuer had to cooperate.

sample.note: The checks ran over the whole set, not a sample.

source.quote: Web certificates are public records, so anyone can check them without asking the issuer.

items.prompt: What should you ask for, so a result does not need your trust?

choices.text: The data, the code and a check you can run

credentials.note: Credentials describe the author. They do not let you re-derive the result.

votes.note: Agreement is another kind of trust. It is not a re-derivation.

source.quote: Ask for the data, the code and a check you can run yourself.
